title: Car Wash in Spain
subtitle: Storyline plan for the readout — ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE

slides.title: Car Wash in Spain
slides.content: Market opportunity and unit economics of a forecourt car wash — ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE

slides.title: Agenda

Spain's paid car-wash market is a ~€[1.1]bn serviceable market growing ~[4]% a year; a forecourt roll-wash of the flagship type pays back in ~[3.8] years at [55] cars/day, so the roll-out case holds if capture reaches ~[4]% of forecourt traffic.
slides.purpose: State the answer and the decision it informs before any exhibit

slides.title: Context
We size Spain's paid car-wash market and test whether one more forecourt wash pays back
slides.content: In scope: paid washes of passenger cars and light vans in Spain — automated roll-over, tunnel, jet-wash bays and hand-wash; Out of scope: fleet/HGV washing, home washing (counted only in TAM), detailing; Geography: Spain, by autonomous community; horizon 2020–2030, annual; €
slides.purpose: The decision is a roll-out count, so the market is sized where the sites are: forecourts · TAM includes home washing to show the whitespace paid formats can convert
slides.image_prompt: Flat vector illustration, navy and light blue on white: a forecourt with a single automated car-wash bay beside fuel pumps, a small car entering; clean lines, no text.

slides.title: Public data covers the car parc and fuel-site network well; wash frequency and ticket rest on surveys
slides.content: Strong: DGT car parc by province; fuel-station census (MITECO); supermarket forecourt counts; Moderate: operator counts and revenues for the main chains (filings, press); Thin: paid-wash frequency and ticket — consumer surveys and the flagship's own data
slides.data: DGT, MITECO, operator filings, consumer survey, aqmen
slides.purpose: Where data is thin we estimate transparently and show the sensitivity · Flagship data is the best evidence on capture and ticket; eight weeks is short

slides.title: The numbers hold up against simple ratios: ~€[45] per car per year and ~[60] washes per site per day
slides.content: €[1.1]bn / [25]m cars = ~€[45] per car per year, or about one wash every six weeks at €[8]; ~[9,000] wash sites nationally → ~[140]m washes / 9,000 / 300 days ≈ [52] washes per site per day; A tunnel at 60 washes/day for 12 hours is one car every 12 minutes — plausible for a forecourt, low for a dedicated chain
slides.purpose: Per-site throughput is consistent with the flagship's observed ~[48] cars/day · If anything the site count is high, which would lift throughput per site

slides.title: If subscriptions reach ~[20]% of users by 2030, the SAM is ~€[1.5]bn rather than €[1.35]bn
slides.content: Standalone chains and fuel retailers push unlimited plans; subscribers wash [2.5]× as often; Overrides vs Base (quantitative):; Washes / car / yr 2030: [11.5] (was [10.1])
slides.purpose: Volume up, ticket down: the net is +[11]% on SAM · Forecourts only benefit if they run their own plan

slides.title: Competition
Five archetypes compete for the wash: fuel retailers, standalone chains, hand-wash networks, supermarkets and independents
slides.content: Integrated fuel retailers — [Client], [Competitor A], [Competitor B]: traffic-led, wash as an add-on to fuel and shop; Standalone automated chains — [Chain A], [Chain B]: quality- and subscription-led, destination sites; Hand-wash networks — [Network A]: labour-based, car-park and mall locations
slides.purpose: The economics differ by archetype, so benchmarks are within archetype · Fuel retailers and standalone chains contest the same premium customer
slides.image_prompt: Flat vector, navy/blue: five distinct storefront silhouettes side by side — fuel forecourt, standalone wash tunnel, hand-wash tent, supermarket, small independent garage; no text.

slides.title: The named players reconcile bottom-up to ~€[1.06]bn, close to the demand-side SAM
slides.content: Player revenue build — revenue × % addressable = car-wash revenue, €m
slides.exhibit: Revenue build: Player revenue build — revenue × % addressable = car-wash revenue, €m
slides.exhibit_title: Player revenue build — revenue × % addressable = car-wash revenue, €m
slides.data: Operator filings, company websites, expert interviews, aqmen
slides.purpose: Fuel retailers hold ~[36]% between three players; standalone chains ~[21]% · Independents are a third of the market and the least visible — the conversion opportunity

slides.title: Archetypes separate on network reach and service depth; fuel retailers are broad and shallow, chains narrow and deep
slides.content: Competitive landscape positioning
slides.purpose: The whitespace is top-right: national reach with premium service — nobody holds it · A fuel retailer with a subscription programme moves right without losing reach

slides.title: Standalone chains are consolidating and opening next to high-traffic forecourts; supermarkets compete on price only
slides.content: [Chain A] acquired [n] regional operators in 2024–25; PE-backed, targeting [300] sites; New sites cluster within 1 km of top-decile forecourts — direct capture risk; Supermarkets hold price at €[5–6] and do not invest in equipment
slides.data: Press, operator announcements, expert interviews, aqmen
slides.purpose: The threat is specific: a chain opening next to a good forecourt · Price competition from supermarkets does not reach the premium customer

slides.title: Convenience and quality decide the wash; price ranks last for the premium customer
slides.content: Key buying factors
slides.purpose: Fuel retailers win convenience by default; quality and loyalty are the gaps to close · Interviews rank convenience > quality > loyalty > speed > price

slides.title: A fuel retailer that matches chain quality and runs a subscription owns the whitespace; the risk is site-by-site entry
slides.content: Whitespace: national reach + premium equipment + subscription — no archetype holds all three; Threat: standalone entry next to the best forecourts; mitigate with site selection and first-mover roll-out; So-what for the roll-out: prioritise sites with high traffic and no chain within 1.5 km
slides.purpose: The roll-out case is a race for the best sites · Subscription is the lever that turns traffic into frequency

slides.title: Coverage is strong on networks and pricing, thin on chain revenues and on independents
slides.content: Strong: site counts, list prices, formats — observed; Moderate: chain revenues — filings for two, estimates for the rest; Weak: independents — count from the fuel-site census, revenue estimated
slides.purpose: Sparse cells are stated, not hidden · Independents' share is directional

slides.title: Company
One roll-wash of the flagship type costs ~€[350]k and reaches maturity in year 2
slides.content: Capex €[350]k: equipment €[220]k, civil works and water recycling €[100]k, permits and signage €[30]k — CLIENT INPUT; Ramp-up: [60]% of mature volume in year 1, [90]% in year 2, mature from year 3; Asset life 10 years; maintenance capex [3]% of equipment per year
slides.exhibit: Text slide: What is being built
slides.purpose: Inputs from the client are separated from aqmen assumptions throughout · Opportunity cost of the forecourt space is included; the case is not flattered

slides.title: Site EBITDA is cars/day × ticket less ~€[1.6] variable per wash and ~€[95]k fixed — volume is the lever

slides.exhibit: Driver tree: One forecourt car wash — unit-economics tree (mature year)
slides.exhibit_title: One forecourt car wash — unit-economics tree (mature year)
slides.purpose: Cars/day is the only low-certainty leaf and the one the client can act on · Costs are observable; the argument is about volume

slides.title: [55] cars/day is a ~[4]% capture of ~[1,400] daily forecourt vehicles — the flagship is at [3.1]% after eight weeks
slides.content: Forecourt traffic ~[1,400] vehicles/day (fuel + shop) — CLIENT INPUT; Capture rate [4]% at maturity → [56] washes/day; flagship trend [2.2]% → [3.1]% over weeks 1–8; Cross-check vs market: [55]/day × 300 = [16.5]k washes ≈ [0.6]% of the regional SAM volume — plausible for one site
slides.purpose: Capture is the assumption to track weekly; [4]% is within the range of comparable forecourt washes · Volume reconciles to the market: no implausible share

slides.title: At maturity a site converts ~€[280]k of revenue into ~€[140]k EBITDA and ~€[133]k cash after maintenance
slides.content: Mature-year P&L per site, €k
slides.purpose: EBITDA margin ~[50]% at maturity; ~[35]% in year 1 during ramp-up · Fixed cost is two-thirds of the cost base — hence the volume sensitivity

slides.title: Cumulative cash turns positive in year [4]: payback ~[3.8] years, IRR ~[22]%, NPV ~€[310]k at [9]%

slides.title: The site covers its fixed costs at ~[28] cars/day and reaches a [15]% IRR at ~[45] — the flagship already clears both

slides.title: Payback stays under [5] years for any ticket above €[7.5] if volume holds at [45]+ cars/day
slides.content: Payback (years) — cars/day × average ticket
slides.exhibit: Sensitivity heatmap: Payback (years) — cars/day × average ticket
slides.purpose: Volume dominates: 10 cars/day ≈ €0.5 of ticket · The case fails the hurdle only below ~[35] cars/day at a sub-€[7.5] ticket

slides.title: Five assertions carry the case; two are already evidenced by the flagship, three need the next six months
slides.content: Capture reaches ~[4]% of forecourt traffic — flagship [3.1]% and rising: PARTLY EVIDENCED; Ticket holds at ~€[8.5] with [30]% premium mix — flagship €[8.7]: EVIDENCED; Cost per wash ~€[1.6] at current water and energy tariffs — supplier quotes: EVIDENCED
slides.exhibit: Text slide: What you need to believe
slides.purpose: The roll-out decision hinges on capture; track it weekly on the flagship · Site selection is the main control over the competitive risk
